analogy.p: A field is like a canteen that students empty every day. Crops eat the N, P and K, so the canteen must be restocked before the next harvest. Phosphate rock is a frozen block nobody can eat until it is thawed and cooked (treated with acid so it becomes soluble). An NPK fertiliser is a ready meal with all three food groups. The analogy breaks down because plants absorb dissolved ions rather than solid food, and surplus food does not simply go to waste: it runs into rivers and causes pollution.

bullets: Recall that N, P and K compounds are used in fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity.
Know that NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of N, P and K.
Know that ammonia can be used to produce ammonium salts and nitric acid.
Know that ammonium nitrate is a salt used as a fertiliser, made from ammonia and nitric acid.
Know that phosphate rock is insoluble and is treated with nitric acid, sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid to make soluble fertiliser salts.
Know that potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are obtained by mining.
Compare industrial production with laboratory preparation of ammonium sulfate (from ammonia solution and sulfuric acid).
Link to the Haber process (source of ammonia) and to titration technique.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This topic sits in the 'Using resources' unit of AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) and is **Chemistry-only (triple) content**. You must know that **compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium** are used in **fertilisers** to improve **agricultural productivity**, and that **NPK fertilisers** are **formulations** (mixtures) of salts containing these elements in appropriate percentages. You must be able to recall how the main fertiliser salts are made, write and recognise the key equations, and **compare the industrial production of a fertiliser with a laboratory preparation** of an ammonium salt. Calculations of relative formula mass and percentage by mass of an element also appear regularly.

bullets: Harvesting removes nutrients permanently from the field, so they must be put back.
N, P and K are called the main plant nutrients because plants need them in relatively large quantities.
Using fertilisers increases yield, which helps feed a growing population from the same land area.
Natural fertilisers (manure, compost) release nutrients slowly and have variable composition.
Manufactured fertilisers contain known, measured percentages of N, P and K, so a farmer can apply exactly the amount needed.
Fertilisers are applied regularly (usually every growing season) because the soil is depleted each time a crop is grown.
Key link: this is applied chemistry, using reactions of acids, alkalis and salts to make useful products.
core.p: Growing plants take **nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium** out of the soil in large amounts. When a crop is harvested and taken away, those elements leave the field with it instead of returning to the soil as they would in natural ecosystems when plants die and rot. If they are not replaced, soil fertility falls year after year and **crop yield** drops. A **fertiliser** is a substance added to soil to replace or increase the supply of these elements, which raises **agricultural productivity** (more food per hectare). This matters because the world population is growing and there is only a limited area of farmland.

bullets: Nitrogen (N): protein and chlorophyll synthesis; promotes green, leafy growth.
Phosphorus (P): root development and energy transfer; part of DNA and cell membranes.
Potassium (K): enzyme function; flowers and fruit; helps resistance to disease.
Plants absorb these elements as dissolved ions (for example NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻, K⁺) through the roots.
A fertiliser is chosen to match the crop: leafy crops like grass need more N, fruiting crops need more K.
An element in short supply is a limiting factor for growth, so adding the missing one raises yield.
Link to biology: these are the mineral ions in the plant nutrition topics.
core.h: The job of each element: N, P and K
core.p: Each of the three elements has a different role in the plant, which is why a balanced fertiliser contains all of them. **Nitrogen** is needed to make **proteins** and **chlorophyll**, so it drives leaf and stem growth. **Phosphorus** is needed for healthy **roots** and for **energy transfer** inside cells, and it forms part of DNA and cell membranes. **Potassium** is needed for the correct functioning of **enzymes** and supports flower and fruit development and disease resistance. A shortage of any one of them limits growth, even if the other two are plentiful.

bullets: Soluble means the compound dissolves in water to release ions that roots can absorb.
Phosphate rock (mainly calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂) is insoluble, so on its own it releases phosphate far too slowly.
Ammonium salts (ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, ammonium phosphate) are all soluble.
Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are soluble and so can be used as they are mined.
Exam wording: 'phosphate rock is insoluble in water so plants cannot absorb it'.
Soluble also means leachable: rain can wash nutrients out of the soil into rivers and lakes.
Higher thinking: the same solubility that makes fertilisers effective makes them a pollution risk.
core.h: Why fertiliser compounds must be soluble
core.p: Plant roots can only take up nutrients when they are **dissolved in water** in the soil as ions. A compound that does not dissolve cannot be absorbed, however much of the element it contains. This is the single most important idea in the whole topic: it explains why **phosphate rock cannot be used directly** (it is insoluble) and why it has to be reacted with an acid first. It is also why heavy rain washes soluble fertilisers out of the soil, which causes pollution of rivers and lakes.

bullets: Ammonia (NH₃) is made in the Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (see the Haber process topic).
Ammonia solution is an alkali, so it neutralises acids to form ammonium salts and water only (no gas given off).
Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.
Ammonia + sulfuric acid → ammonium sulfate: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Ammonia + phosphoric acid → ammonium phosphate, which supplies both N and P.
Nitric acid can itself be manufactured from ammonia, so ammonia is the key raw material.
These are neutralisation-type reactions, so the same ideas as acid plus alkali apply.
core.p: The main source of nitrogen for fertilisers is **ammonia**, NH₃, which is manufactured on a huge scale by the **Haber process** from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen from natural gas. Ammonia is a gas that dissolves in water to give an **alkaline** solution. It can be reacted with acids to make **ammonium salts**, and it can also be used to produce **nitric acid**. Because nitric acid is itself made from ammonia, ammonia is the starting point for almost all nitrogen fertilisers. You do not need the detailed steps of converting ammonia into nitric acid, only that it can be done.

bullets: Formula: NH₄NO₃. Relative formula mass = 14 + (4 × 1) + 14 + (3 × 16) = 80.
Percentage of nitrogen = (2 × 14) ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%.
Neutralisation of an alkali (ammonia) by an acid (nitric acid) gives a salt only.
Contains nitrogen as both NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions, so it provides N for the plant fast.
Soluble in water, so absorbed by roots at once but also easily washed out by rain.
Made continuously in industry; the neutralisation is exothermic and the heat is used.
The two reactants (ammonia and nitric acid) both ultimately come from ammonia, so the supply of ammonia controls the cost.
core.p: **Ammonium nitrate**, NH₄NO₃, is a very popular fertiliser because it contains nitrogen in two forms (the ammonium ion and the nitrate ion) and has a high percentage of nitrogen by mass, **35%**. It is made by reacting **ammonia** with **nitric acid**: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. On an industrial scale the reaction is carried out continuously in large vessels, and the heat released by the neutralisation is used to evaporate water from the product. The resulting salt is soluble, so it dissolves in soil water and is quickly available to the plant.

bullets: Step 1: use a pipette to measure 25.0 cm³ of ammonia solution into a conical flask and add a few drops of a suitable indicator.
Step 2: add dilute sulfuric acid from a burette, swirling, until the indicator just changes colour (the end-point). Record the volume.
Step 3: repeat with exactly the same volumes of alkali and acid but with no indicator, so the salt is pure.
Step 4: heat the solution gently in an evaporating basin until crystals just start to form at the edge (the point of crystallisation); do not evaporate to dryness.
Step 5: leave the solution to cool and crystallise, filter off the crystals, wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter paper or in a warm oven.
Equation: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Reason for titration: it finds the exact quantities for neutralisation so no excess acid or alkali is left.
Reason for cold wash: the crystals are soluble, so cold water removes impurities with little loss.
core.p: You must know how to prepare a pure, dry sample of **ammonium sulfate** in the laboratory, because the specification asks you to compare it with industrial production. Ammonia solution (an alkali) is neutralised with dilute sulfuric acid. Because both reactants are soluble, you cannot just filter off a product, so the exact volumes needed are found first by **titration** and the reaction is then repeated **without indicator** to avoid contaminating the product. The solution is then partly evaporated and cooled so that crystals form.

bullets: With nitric acid: phosphate rock + nitric acid → phosphoric acid + calcium nitrate. Balanced: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6HNO₃ → 2H₃PO₄ + 3Ca(NO₃)₂.
With sulfuric acid: phosphate rock + sulfuric acid → calcium sulfate + calcium phosphate (called single superphosphate). Balanced with the real product: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2CaSO₄ + Ca(H₂PO₄)₂.
With phosphoric acid: phosphate rock + phosphoric acid → calcium phosphate (called triple superphosphate). Balanced: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 4H₃PO₄ → 3Ca(H₂PO₄)₂.
In the exam, use the product names in the specification wording; the soluble product is a 'calcium phosphate' in this context.
The nitric acid route also gives calcium nitrate, which is itself a source of nitrogen.
The phosphoric acid made in the nitric acid route can be neutralised with ammonia to make ammonium phosphate, giving N and P together.
Triple superphosphate contains more phosphorus per kg than single because it has no calcium sulfate diluting it.
core.p: **Phosphate rock** is mined and is mostly **calcium phosphate**, Ca₃(PO₄)₂. It is **insoluble** in water, so it is no use as a fertiliser until it has been treated. Reacting it with an acid converts the insoluble phosphate into soluble compounds that plants can use. The specification gives three treatments, using **nitric acid**, **sulfuric acid** or **phosphoric acid**, each giving a different product mixture. The choice of acid depends on what the fertiliser is for and the cost.

bullets: Potassium chloride (KCl) and potassium sulfate (K₂SO₄) are the two compounds named in the spec.
Both are soluble in water, so no treatment with acid is required.
They are extracted by mining rock salt-type deposits, then crushed and purified.
Potassium is the K in NPK, from the Latin 'kalium'.
Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) supplies both K and N, so it is a useful two-nutrient fertiliser.
Mined resources are finite, so potassium and phosphate rock are non-renewable and need careful use.
Link to resources: this is part of the 'Using resources' unit on finite raw materials.
core.p: Unlike nitrogen compounds (made from air and natural gas) and phosphates (treated with acid), the potassium compounds used in fertilisers are simply **obtained by mining**. **Potassium chloride**, KCl, and **potassium sulfate**, K₂SO₄, occur in underground deposits and are dug out, purified and used directly because they are already **soluble**. This makes the potassium part of an NPK fertiliser the least chemically processed. Mining has an environmental cost because it uses land and energy, but needs no chemical reaction.

bullets: A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, with each component in a controlled amount.
Ingredients can include ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate, ammonium sulfate, potassium chloride and potassium sulfate.
Ammonium phosphate and potassium nitrate each supply more than one of the three elements.
Bags show three numbers for N, P and K content so a farmer can match the product to the crop.
Different crops and soils need different proportions: grass needs more N, fruit crops more K.
Mixtures are not chemically bonded together, so the individual salts keep their own properties.
Formulation is a general term for any designed mixture (fuels, medicines, alloys, paints, fertilisers).
core.p: An **NPK fertiliser** is a **formulation**: a carefully designed mixture of several salts, each present in a measured proportion, so that the product contains **N, P and K** in the **appropriate percentages** for a given crop. Typical ingredients are an ammonium salt for nitrogen, a soluble phosphate for phosphorus and potassium chloride for potassium. Mixing the salts means the farmer can supply all three nutrients in one application. The composition is shown on the bag so the farmer can choose a product to suit the crop and soil.

bullets: Scale: industry makes tonnes per day; the laboratory makes grams.
Process type: industry is continuous (reactants fed in, product removed all the time); the laboratory is a batch process (one lot at a time).
Controlling quantities: industry uses flow-rate control and sensors; the lab uses a pipette, burette and titration.
Purity: laboratory samples aim for pure crystals; industrial fertilisers are less pure and are formulated.
Raw materials: industry uses large supplies of ammonia, acids and mined rock; the lab uses bottled reagents.
Energy and cost: the industrial plant has high set-up (capital) costs but a low cost per tonne; lab cost per gram is high.
Industry recycles heat from exothermic neutralisation; the lab does not.
Industry also considers environmental impact, safety and the transport of products.
core.p: The specification asks you to **compare** the two. The same reaction (ammonia and an acid) is used, but the **scale, method and aims** differ. In industry, fertilisers are made in thousands of tonnes per year, using **continuous** processes with automatic control, because large quantities of cheap product are needed. In the laboratory only a small, very pure sample is made, using **batch** methods and measured volumes. A good comparison always mentions scale, type of process, how the quantities are measured, purity and cost.

bullets: Ar values used: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32, K = 39, P = 31.
The higher the %N, the less mass is needed to supply a given mass of nitrogen.
For reacting masses: moles = mass ÷ Mr, use the equation ratio, then mass = moles × Mr.
core.p: Fertiliser questions often involve **relative formula mass (Mr)** and **percentage by mass** of an element. Percentage of an element in a compound = (number of atoms × Ar ÷ Mr of compound) × 100. This lets you compare how much nitrogen different fertilisers deliver per kg, a key factor in cost. You also meet **reacting mass** calculations from a balanced equation, for example the mass of ammonium sulfate made from a given mass of ammonia. Always show Mr working and units, as marks are given for method.

bullets: Eutrophication is caused by excess nitrates and phosphates entering water.
Chain: run-off → nutrient build-up → algal bloom → light blocked → plants die → decomposers use up oxygen → fish die.
Farmers reduce the risk by using the right amount, not applying before heavy rain, and not spreading near water.
Nitrates in drinking water can also be a health concern, so water companies must treat it.
Over-use of fertiliser wastes money for the farmer.
Mining potassium and phosphate rock damages habitats and uses energy.
Make links: bacteria respiration uses oxygen, so it is an aerobic process in the water.
core.p: Too much fertiliser causes pollution. Rain washes unused soluble nitrates and phosphates off fields (**run-off** or **leaching**) into rivers and lakes. These nutrients cause algae to grow very quickly, an **algal bloom**, which blocks light from reaching plants below. The plants die, and bacteria decompose them, using up **dissolved oxygen**. With too little oxygen, fish and other aquatic animals die. This whole process is called **eutrophication**. It is a common 6-mark 'explain' question.

bullets: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, 450 °C, 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst; unreacted gases are recycled.
Titration: accurate measuring with a pipette and burette; concordant results within 0.10 cm³.
Crystallisation: evaporate to the point of crystallisation, then cool slowly for larger crystals.
Percentage yield and atom economy can be asked about for fertiliser reactions.
Reacting masses use the mole equation moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Biology links: nitrate uptake, protein synthesis, food chains, eutrophication.
Evaluating: compare cost, yield, purity and environmental impact when given data.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: This topic connects several parts of the course, which is how it is tested in longer questions. The nitrogen comes from the **Haber process**, so questions may ask you to explain conditions or yield. The lab preparation reuses **titration** skills and the idea of **crystallisation**. The percentage composition links to **relative formula mass**, and the environmental part links to biology (**eutrophication**, food webs) and to **sustainability**. At Higher tier you are expected to use balanced equations, reacting masses and to justify choices using data about cost and yield.

exam: Command words: 'State' gets 1 mark for a fact (for example 'phosphate rock is insoluble'); 'Explain' needs a reason using 'because' or 'so that'.
1-mark recall: 'Name the three elements in NPK fertiliser' → nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium (all three needed).
2-mark explain: 'Why is phosphate rock treated with acid?' → it is insoluble (1) so the acid converts it to a soluble salt that plants can absorb (1).
Equations: for 2 marks write the correct formulae first, then balance; show state symbols only if asked.
Calculation of %N: show Ar, Mr, then the percentage; always give the units (%) and correct significant figures.
Reacting-mass questions: moles = mass ÷ Mr, use the ratio from the equation, then convert back to mass.
Lab preparation 4–6 mark questions: use a numbered sequence: titration with indicator, repeat without indicator, evaporate to crystallisation point, cool, filter, dry.
Comparison questions: use comparative words ('whereas', 'in contrast') for each point, covering scale, process type, purity and cost.
6-mark eutrophication: write a clear sequence of 5–6 linked steps in order, ending with the death of fish due to lack of oxygen.
Data questions: compare the %N of fertilisers and link to cost per kg of nitrogen.
Use the words 'soluble', 'insoluble', 'ions', 'neutralisation' and 'formulation' exactly; the mark scheme looks for them.
Remember Chemistry-only content: if you sit the separate Chemistry paper, it is examined in Paper 2.

mistakes.r: It is insoluble in water, so plants cannot absorb it. It must be treated with acid to make soluble salts.
mistakes.w: Phosphate rock can be used directly as fertiliser.

mistakes.r: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. Fertilisers supply mineral ions, absorbed dissolved in water.
mistakes.w: Fertilisers are 'plant food' that plants eat.

mistakes.r: Plants cannot use N₂ from the air. They need soluble nitrogen compounds such as ammonium and nitrate ions.
mistakes.w: Nitrogen in fertilisers is nitrogen gas.

mistakes.r: Repeat the neutralisation without indicator so that the crystals are not contaminated by the indicator.
mistakes.w: Not removing the indicator in the lab preparation.

mistakes.r: Heat only to the point of crystallisation, then cool to crystallise, filter and dry. Heating to dryness may decompose the salt and spoils crystals.
The sequence is: nutrients, algal bloom, light blocked, plants die, bacteria use oxygen, fish die from lack of oxygen.
In the lab it is made from ammonia SOLUTION (an alkali) and dilute sulfuric acid, using titration.
mistakes.w: Ammonium sulfate is made from ammonia gas and sulfuric acid in the lab, in a closed flask.

mistakes.r: Compare scale, continuous v batch, control of quantities, purity, cost and energy use.
mistakes.w: Industrial and laboratory methods are the same, only bigger.

summary: You must know why N, P and K compounds are used as fertilisers, how ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, treated phosphate rock and mined potassium salts supply them, and how NPK fertilisers are formulations. You must also compare industrial and laboratory production and do related calculations, because this explains how chemistry raises crop yield and what pollution it can cause.

terms.d: A substance added to soil to replace or increase the supply of elements such as N, P and K, improving crop yield.
The amount of crop produced from a given area of land.
A formulation of salts containing the appropriate percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
A mixture designed as a useful product, with each component in a measured amount.
A mined rock containing calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, which is insoluble in water.
Able to dissolve in water to form a solution.
NH₄NO₃, a soluble salt made from ammonia and nitric acid, used as a nitrogen fertiliser.
(NH₄)₂SO₄, a soluble salt made from ammonia solution and sulfuric acid.
The reaction of an acid with an alkali to form a salt and water.
A method of finding the exact volumes of acid and alkali that react together, using an indicator.
The point at which an indicator changes colour, showing the acid and alkali have exactly neutralised each other.
A process in which reactants are fed in and product is removed all the time.
A process in which a fixed amount is made in one go, then the equipment is emptied and restarted.
Excess nutrients in water cause algal bloom, loss of light and oxygen, and death of aquatic life.
Water that flows over the land, carrying dissolved fertiliser into rivers and lakes.
The product of treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid: calcium sulfate and calcium phosphate.
The product of treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid: calcium phosphate.

worked.q: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16) [3 marks]
steps: Mass of nitrogen in one formula unit = 2 × 14 = 28

worked.q: Ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium sulfate made from 3.4 g of ammonia. (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32) [4 marks]
steps: Mr of NH₃ = 14 + 3 = 17; moles of NH₃ = 3.4 ÷ 17 = 0.20 mol
Ratio 2 NH₃ : 1 (NH₄)₂SO₄, so moles of (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10 mol

worked.ans: Model answer: Both use ammonia solution neutralised by an acid. In industry the reaction is continuous and on a huge scale, with quantities controlled automatically and heat recycled, whereas in the laboratory it is a small batch process where titration with an indicator gives the exact volumes, the reaction is repeated without indicator, and the pure crystals are obtained by evaporating to the crystallisation point, cooling, filtering and drying.
worked.q: Compare the industrial production of ammonium nitrate with the laboratory preparation of ammonium sulfate. [6 marks]
steps: Both involve neutralising ammonia (an alkali) with an acid to give a soluble ammonium salt.
Scale: industry makes thousands of tonnes; the lab makes a few grams.
Type: industry uses a continuous process; the lab uses a batch process.
Controlling quantities: industry uses automatic flow control; the lab uses a pipette and burette with an indicator to find the volumes, then repeats without indicator.
Purity: the lab aims for pure crystals by evaporating, cooling, filtering and drying; industry makes a formulated product.
Cost and energy: industry has high capital cost but low cost per tonne, and uses the heat from neutralisation.
